common_name: Blue Echeveria (Hardy Hen and Chicks Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Separate rooted offsets from the mother rosette in spring and let cut surfaces callus for a day or two before setting them into gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: One of the cold-hardier members of the genus, Echeveria secunda forms tight blue-grey rosettes that steadily produce offsets, quickly building into a dense mounding cluster or living mat. It shrugs off light frost better than most Echeverias and tolerates brief winter dips that would damage more tender species, though a dry overhead cover still prevents rot in wet climates. Plant in gritty, mineral soil and let it dry fully between waterings, since the tightly packed rosettes hold moisture at their base longer than more open-growing types. Coral-pink and yellow flower spikes rise above the foliage in late winter to spring, drawing hummingbirds.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Cante Echeveria (Ghostly Pale Blue-White Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Start from leaf cuttings or rooted offsets in spring, allowing cut ends to callus before placing in fast-draining succulent mix.

directions: Discovered on the cliffs of north-central Mexico, Echeveria cante forms one of the largest and most dramatic rosettes in the genus, with thick, chalky, pale lavender-white leaves that can reach over a foot across at maturity. The heavy farina coating gives the whole plant an almost sculptural, frosted look, and the leaf margins blush coral-pink under bright light and cool temperatures. Keep the farina intact by watering at the soil line rather than overhead and avoid handling the leaves, since any contact leaves a permanent mark. It stays mostly solitary for years before offsetting, so plan on generous spacing from the start.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Painted Lady Echeveria (Derenberg's Clustering Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Detach rooted offsets from the base of the clump in spring and pot them individually in gritty succulent mix once calloused.

directions: Native to the dry ridges of Oaxaca, Echeveria derenbergii forms small, tightly packed blue-green rosettes tipped in red, three-pointed leaf ends that give the species its distinctive look. It clusters readily from the base, quickly filling a shallow pot or rock crevice with dozens of tiny rosettes, and it is one of the most reliable winter bloomers in the genus, sending up bright orange-yellow flowers on short stems. Full sun keeps the rosettes tight and colorful, while too much shade causes stretching and loss of the red leaf tips. Because it stays compact, it is a favorite for dish gardens and rock walls where larger Echeverias would outgrow the space.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Propagate from leaf cuttings or the occasional basal offset, letting the wound dry before rooting in lean, mineral succulent mix.

directions: A diminutive collector's species from Oaxaca, Echeveria purpusorum forms flat, triangular, olive-green leaves marked with distinctive maroon-purple spotting and a slightly warty texture unlike the smooth foliage of most Echeverias. It stays small and mostly solitary for a long time, making it well suited to shallow pans and miniature succulent arrangements rather than mass planting. Bright, direct light intensifies both the spotting and the reddish leaf margins, while low light quickly causes the rosette to stretch and lose its compact form. It is slow to offset, so patient propagation from individual leaves is the most dependable way to build stock.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Remove rooted offsets in spring and let cut surfaces callus for a couple of days before setting into fast-draining succulent mix.

directions: Sometimes sold in the trade under the synonym Echeveria desmetiana, this Mexican species carries powdery, silvery-blue-white leaves finished with a fine pink edge that deepens in strong light and cool weather. It clusters steadily, forming a low colony of offsets around the original rosette and works well massed as a groundcover in raised beds or containers. The dense farina coating is easily marred by handling or overhead irrigation, so water at the soil surface and keep foot traffic away from established clumps. Coral-red, bell-shaped flowers appear on arching stems in spring, held well above the foliage.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and let the cut base callus for a day or two before planting into gritty succulent mix.

directions: This compact hybrid cultivar is grown for the deep cocoa-brown to aubergine coloration that develops across its thick, close-packed leaves under strong sun and cool nights, a color that fades toward olive-green with more shade or warmth. The tight rosette form holds up well in containers and mixed succulent bowls, where its dark tone provides contrast against the blues and greens of companion Echeverias. Like other richly pigmented cultivars, it needs bright, unfiltered light to maintain its color and will stretch and green up if kept indoors or in low light. Offsets form slowly at the base, so most growers propagate by carefully removing and rooting individual leaves.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
